entry.title: How to Turn a PDF Page Into a Clickable Preview in HTML
entry.summary: Save one PDF page as a JPG and link the preview to the full document in HTML. Try it with a downloadable two-page café menu and a working website example.
entry.content:
Show the first page of a PDF as a small picture on your website. When a visitor clicks the picture or the words below it, they get the complete document.

Try the café menu on your phone or computer. The preview shows Breakfast & lunch. Tap it to find Drinks & sweets on page two. Open the finished café page.

Start with the practice files​

You'll need a browser and a text editor. Download the café menu project and extract the ZIP. Open the folder that contains cafe-menu.html, menu.pdf and menu-preview.jpg. To make the preview yourself, copy just cafe-menu.html and menu.pdf into a new folder. You'll add the JPG there next.

For your own website, use the HTML page you want visitors to see and put your PDF beside it. You can also download the two-page practice PDF on its own.

How to save PDF as JPG in your browser​

  1. Open the Phoenix Code PDF to JPG Converter. Select Choose PDF and open menu.pdf. Two page previews appear.
  2. Under Resolution, choose Custom. Set Size by to Pixels, enter 600 in Width (px) and leave Height (px) empty. The converter keeps the proportions of your page.
  3. Under Pages to export, enter 1. Check that the tool says 1 of 2 pages selected. Only the breakfast page should be checked.
  4. Select Convert selected pages. When page one says Ready to download, select its Download JPG button. The practice file downloads as menu-page-1.jpg, at 600 × 800 pixels.
  5. Rename the download to menu-preview.jpg and move it beside cafe-menu.html and menu.pdf. Open the JPG to check that it shows the café name and the breakfast menu.

Link the image and its caption to the PDF​

Open cafe-menu.html in your text editor. In the practice file, find this link just below </header>. On your own page, insert it inside <body> where the preview should appear.

<a class="menu-link" href="menu.pdf">
  <img src="menu-preview.jpg" alt="" width="600" height="800">
  <span>Read the full menu (PDF)</span>
</a>

src names the picture the browser shows. href names the file the link opens. If your document is called lunch-menu.pdf, use href="lunch-menu.pdf" and keep src pointed at your JPG. Change the caption to tell visitors which document opens.

Because the picture and the visible caption are inside the same link, a keyboard user reaches them in one tab stop. The caption already names the destination, so the image has an empty alt="". W3C guidance on images within links.

The practice page already has the following layout rules. On your own page, add them to your stylesheet or inside a <style> element in <head>. If you use a different JPG, update the HTML width and height to match its pixel dimensions.

.menu-link {
  display: inline-flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  gap: 0.75rem;
  width: fit-content;
  max-width: 100%;
}

.menu-link img {
  display: block;
  width: 18rem;
  max-width: 100%;
  height: auto;
}

Check the full menu​

Save cafe-menu.html and open it in your browser. Click the picture. Depending on your browser settings, the PDF opens in a viewer or downloads. Open the file and check that page two contains Drinks & sweets and Lemon cake. Go back to the HTML page and try the caption. With a keyboard, press Tab until the menu link has a focus outline, then press Enter.

If the caption works but the picture is missing, compare src with the JPG's filename and folder. If the picture appears but the PDF fails to open, check href against the PDF's name. When you put the page online, include all three files and test the live link from your phone. For a link to another HTML page, see Link to another page in Phoenix Code.

entry.title: Convert a Word document to Markdown and check the headings and table
entry.summary: Convert a Word .docx to GitHub Flavored Markdown with Pandoc. Preview the saved file and check its heading levels, table values, and a pipe inside a cell.
entry.content:
Pandoc can turn a Word document into a Markdown file you can use in a GitHub README. One command creates the file. Opening it in a preview lets you check that your headings and table cells survived.

Try it with a walk plan. One meeting point is Gate A | East car park. Markdown uses that same vertical bar to separate table cells, so that address gives you an easy way to check your result.

Convert the Word file with Pandoc​

  1. Download the practice Word document, or use a .docx of your own. Open it and note the headings and the two rows of walk details.
  2. Install Pandoc for your operating system. Open a new Terminal or PowerShell window and run pandoc --version. You should see a version number. Pandoc installation instructions.
  3. Change to the folder where you saved the Word file. For example, if you saved it in Downloads and your terminal starts in your home folder, run cd Downloads. For a different location, type cd, a space, and the full folder path in double quotes.
  4. Run the command below. It writes weekend-walk-plan.md beside the Word file. The gfm setting selects GitHub Flavored Markdown, which supports tables. For your own file, change both filenames and choose a new output name if you already have a Markdown copy you want to keep.
pandoc "weekend-walk-plan.docx" -f docx -t gfm -o "weekend-walk-plan.md"

Open the saved Markdown and check the table​

Open the Phoenix Code Markdown Viewer. Choose Open file and select weekend-walk-plan.md from the same folder. On a narrow screen, tap Preview to see the formatted document.

  • Headings. The source begins with # Saturday walks. The two hashes in ## Meeting points put it one level below Saturday walks.
  • Meeting time. The source reads **9 am**. The preview shows 9 am in bold.
  • Table. Look for three columns. The 4 km Woodland loop meets at Gate A | East car park, all in one cell. The 12 km River path meets at Footbridge. In the source, \| keeps the bar inside the address.

If the end of an address disappears from a cell, open the .md in a text editor, put a backslash before the bar inside the address, and save. Open the saved file again in the viewer. You can compare it with the Markdown file produced from the example. For more on alignment and separators, see Make a Markdown table with aligned columns.

Restore the Word title if your README needs it​

In the Word document, Weekend walk plan uses the built-in Title style. Pandoc reads it as document metadata, so the command above leaves it out of the Markdown body.

To include the title, open the saved .md in a text editor. Insert # Weekend walk plan at the top, followed by a blank line. Change # Saturday walks to ## Saturday walks and ## Meeting points to ### Meeting points. Save and reopen the file in the viewer. The title should now sit above both sections, with the route details still in their original cells.

entry.title: How to Add a Favicon in HTML
entry.summary: Add a favicon to your HTML pages, choose the right icon path for a site in a subfolder, and check it from a browser tab.
entry.content:
A favicon is the small picture beside a page title in a browser tab. To add one, put the icon file on your website and add a <link rel="icon"> inside each page’s <head>. The href tells the browser where to find the file.

You’ll need an HTML page you can edit and a logo, or you can use the sample image below. We’ll give a site called Trail Notes the same icon on its home page and its About page, one folder deeper.

Make the icon files​

  1. Open the free Phoenix Code Favicon Generator. Click Choose image to open a PNG, JPG, or WebP file. To follow along without artwork, click Try a sample.
  2. Look at Light tab and Dark tab. Both show the icon at 16 × 16 pixels. If the lettering disappears at this size, try a single letter or a simpler shape.
  3. Click Download icons and extract favicon.zip. Copy favicon.ico, favicon-96x96.png, and apple-touch-icon.png into the folder that holds your home page. The ZIP also includes a README.txt you can keep for reference.

Link the files from each HTML page​

In the generator, scroll to Add it to your website and click Copy HTML. The links start with /, which means the top of your domain. Check the address where your icon will be published before pasting them.

Where the icon file opensWhat to use
https://example.com/favicon.icoUse the generator’s HTML as copied.
https://example.com/trail-notes/favicon.icoAdd /trail-notes/ before each filename as shown below. Substitute your own public folder name.

For the second case, the project folder contains these files.

trail-notes/
├── index.html
├── favicon.ico
├── favicon-96x96.png
├── apple-touch-icon.png
└── guides/
    └── about.html

Open index.html in your editor. Place these three lines just before </head>. If the page already has icon links, update their paths. Do the same in guides/about.html, then save both files and publish them along with the icons.

<link rel="icon" href="/trail-notes/favicon.ico" sizes="16x16 32x32 48x48">
<link rel="icon" type="image/png" href="/trail-notes/favicon-96x96.png" sizes="96x96">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/trail-notes/apple-touch-icon.png" sizes="180x180">

The first two links give browsers a choice of tab icons. The last supplies the icon for an Apple home-screen shortcut. Both HTML pages can use the same links because each address starts at the domain root.

Check the icon on both pages​

  1. Open the published home page in its own browser tab. Look to the left of its title for your icon.
  2. Open the nested About page in a second tab. It should show the same icon. If only the home page works, look for href="favicon.ico" on the About page. That spelling makes the browser look for guides/favicon.ico. Use the shared path from the example.
  3. If the icon is missing on both pages, open its address directly on your own domain. For Trail Notes, that path is /trail-notes/favicon-96x96.png. You should see the image. A missing-page message or your site’s home page means the image is unavailable at that address.

If the image opens directly but the tab still shows an old icon, try a fresh private window. To see which icon URL the browser requested, open developer tools, select Network, and reload the page. Check a failed resource in an HTML preview.

entry.title: How to Change an SVG Icon’s Fill and Stroke Colors
entry.summary: Recolor the inside and outline of an inline SVG separately. Try a trail-marker icon in the Phoenix HTML Editor, then download and reopen the finished page.
entry.content:
To change the color inside an SVG shape, edit its fill. To change the line around it, edit its stroke. Try both on the trail marker below. You’ll start with an orange circle and a white border, then save a green circle with a dark border. The white arrow in the middle keeps its color.

Open the practice icon​

Open the Phoenix HTML Editor. In the index.html tab, replace the example code with the block below. Leave Auto-run on, or click Run after an edit. If your screen shows separate panels, select Preview to see the icon.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head><title>Trail marker</title></head>
<body>
  <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
       width="160" height="160" viewBox="0 0 80 80"
       role="img" aria-label="Trail marker pointing right">
    <circle cx="40" cy="40" r="32"
            fill="#ff8c42" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="6" />
    <path d="M29 40h22m-8-8 8 8-8 8"
          fill="none" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="4"
          stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" />
  </svg>
</body>
</html>

Change one part at a time​

  1. Find the line with <circle. Change its fill from #ff8c42 to #237a58. The disc turns green. The arrow stays white.
  2. On that same circle, change stroke="#ffffff" to stroke="#17382e". A dark green ring appears around the disc. Keep stroke-width="6" so the outline stays visible.
  3. Look at the <path beneath the circle. This is the arrow. Its fill="none" keeps its interior empty, and its white stroke draws the line. To recolor only the arrow in your own version, edit the stroke on this path.

Click Download (the downward arrow) in the editor toolbar. Open the downloaded index.html in your browser. The green disc, dark ring, and white arrow should appear in that copy too. Open a downloaded HTML page in Chrome

My HTML only shows an image tag​

If the page contains <img src="images/marker.svg" alt="Trail marker">, the shapes live in images/marker.svg. Open that file in your code editor, find the shape, edit its fill or stroke there, and save. Reload the page that uses the image. A CSS fill on the outer <img> won’t reach the circle inside the separate file. SVG fill and stroke

entry.title: How to Compare Two JSON Files and Read the Differences
entry.summary: Compare two JSON files in your browser. Follow a worked example to find added, removed, and changed values and see how array order affects the result.
entry.content:
Did a setting change, or did someone just rearrange the file? Open the old version in Original JSON and the new version in Changed JSON, then click Compare JSON. Phoenix Code compares the values and shows the location of each difference. Spaces, indentation, and the order of keys in an object can change without showing up as edits.

You can use your own two files or paste the examples below. The free JSON Compare & Diff tool runs in your browser.

Compare the old and new settings​

Open JSON Compare & Diff. If you have your own files, click Open file in Original JSON and choose the older file. Then use Open file in Changed JSON to choose the newer one.

To try it with Trail Notes, paste the first block into Original JSON and the second into Changed JSON.

Original JSON

{
  "project": "Trail Notes",
  "published": false,
  "pages": ["home", "walks"],
  "theme": {"color": "green", "logo": "trail.svg"}
}

Changed JSON

{
  "theme": {"color": "green", "accent": "amber"},
  "pages": ["home", "walks", "map"],
  "published": true,
  "project": "Trail Notes"
}

Read what changed​

Click Compare JSON. For Trail Notes, the message reads Compared: 4 differences found. The toolbar shows 2 added · 1 removed · 1 changed.

Use the up and down arrows beside the difference count to move through the results. Each stop gives you a path. For example, /pages/2 means the third item in pages, because array positions start at zero.

PathWhat happened in Trail Notes
/publishedThe existing setting changed from false to true.
/pages/2"map" was added after "walks".
/theme/logoThe logo field and its value "trail.svg" were removed.
/theme/accentA new accent field was added with the value "amber".

Click Copy differences to keep a text report. It uses + for an addition, - for a removal, and ~ for a changed value. If an addition shows up as a removal, check which version you opened in Original JSON.

Why moving a key is different from moving an array item​

The project key appears first in the original and last in the changed file. Its value is still "Trail Notes", so it has no entry in the report. An object identifies each value by its key.

An array identifies items by position. To see this, replace the original pane with {"pages":["home","walks"]} and the changed pane with {"pages":["walks","home"]}. Click Compare JSON again. You’ll get 2 changed. Position /pages/0 now holds "walks", and /pages/1 now holds "home".

To apply a change, open the source file in your editor, edit that setting, and save. Then open the saved version in Changed JSON and compare again. If you’re editing a project configuration in Phoenix Code, see JSON editing and error checks.

If the comparison stops at a closing bracket, check for an extra comma after the last value. Find and fix a trailing comma in JSON.

entry.title: Build a responsive CSS Grid sidebar that stacks on phones
entry.summary: Make a header, sidebar, and content area in Phoenix’s CSS Grid Generator. Check the layout at two widths and open the finished HTML file in your browser.
entry.content:
A walking guide needs room for a list of walks beside the route description. On a phone, people should be able to read the description without scrolling sideways. You can build both layouts in Phoenix’s free CSS Grid Generator and download a single HTML file that switches between them.

You’ll make three blocks called Trail notes, Walks, and Route details. All you need is a browser.

Set up the sidebar​

  1. Open the CSS Grid Generator. At the top of the builder, choose Sidebar. The first block stretches across the top. The two below it share a row.
  2. Under Selected item, choose Item 1. Change Label to Trail notes and press Tab. Repeat with Item 2 for Walks and Item 3 for Route details. On a phone, open Layout controls to see these fields.
  3. Under Layout, keep Stack on small screens checked. Beside Live preview, open the width menu and choose Desktop · 960px. On a phone, tap Preview & code first.

The preset uses four equal columns. The heading spans all four. Below it, Walks takes the first column and Route details takes the other three.

Check what happens on a phone​

Choose Mobile · 375px from the same menu. Stacked layout appears under the preview. Read from the top down and you should see Trail notes, Walks, then Route details. Each takes the full width available inside the page margins.

Save and try the finished page​

  1. Click Download HTML below the code. Open the downloaded phoenix-grid.html in your browser.
  2. Make the window narrow, then wide again. The exported CSS uses @media (max-width: 640px). At 640 CSS pixels and below you get one column. Above that width the sidebar and content sit side by side.
  3. To use the layout for your own page, open the downloaded file in your editor and find Route details inside <body>. Replace that label with a route description, save, and reload the browser. Keep the three blocks in the order you want people to read them on a phone. The small-screen layout follows their order in the HTML.

If your own content sticks out past the right edge after the columns stack, check whether an item inside the grid has a fixed width. Test a page at different screen sizes.

entry.title: How to Decode Base64 Text and Preview an Encoded Image
entry.summary: Decode a UTF-8 message, check an invalid Base64 string, and display a PNG data URL in an HTML preview. Both examples work in your browser.
entry.content:
If you have a Base64-encoded message, paste it into Base64 Encoded in the Phoenix decoder and click Decode. If you copied something starting with data:image/png;base64, from an HTML file, you have a picture. Here’s how to read the message and see the picture.

Decode a text message​

  1. Open the Phoenix Base64 Encoder & Decoder. Find the box labeled Base64 Encoded.

  2. Copy this whole string into the box, including the two equals signs at the end.

    Q2Fmw6kgYnkgdGhlIHRyYWlsLg==

  3. Click Decode below that box. The Text box should now read Café by the trail. The accent in Café is part of the original UTF-8 text. Click Copy beside Text to keep the readable version.

  4. To check it the other way, click Encode beneath the text. You should get the original string back, including its ending.

If the tool reports Invalid Base64 string, recopy the complete value. For example, Q2Fm% produces that error. Check for punctuation copied from the surrounding sentence or quotation marks from the HTML. A Base64 string by itself doesn’t tell you which kind of file it contains.

See an image copied from HTML​

In a data URL, the part before the comma describes what follows. In data:image/png;base64,..., the type is PNG and the rest represents the image bytes. Keep the prefix and the bytes together when you use the URL as an image source. Data URL syntax

Open the Phoenix HTML Viewer and paste this complete image tag into HTML source. If the Viewer shows tabs, click Preview.

<img width="64" height="64" alt="Green square"
  src="data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAIAAACQd1PeAAAACXBIWXMAAAPoAAAD6AG1e1JrAAAADElEQVQImWPQqwkCAAHYAP0XYDMkAAAAAElFTkSuQmCC">

The preview shows a green square. The example PNG contains one green pixel. The HTML displays it at 64 × 64 so you can see it. If you see a broken-image icon, check that the comma and the start and end of the encoded data all made it inside the quotes. Troubleshoot missing images in an HTML preview

entry.title: How to Change All Caps to Sentence Case on a Website
entry.summary: Fix a heading typed in all caps, or one that CSS displays in uppercase. Try both cases with a short HTML example and check the saved result.
entry.content:
You change a heading to “Meet at the NASA exhibit,” save the file, and the page still shows MEET AT THE NASA EXHIBIT. Open the HTML and look between the heading tags. If the words are uppercase there, edit the text. If they already look right there, check the CSS.

When the letters in the file are all capitals​

  1. Open the Phoenix Case Converter. Paste this example into Your text.

    MEET AT THE NASA EXHIBIT. BRING A MAP.

  2. Under For writing, click Sentence case. The result is Meet at the NASA exhibit. Bring a map. If you choose lowercase instead, you get meet at the nasa exhibit. bring a map. That choice also changes the acronym.

  3. Read through names, initials, and brand spellings before copying. Click Copy, replace only the words between the heading’s opening and closing tags, and save your HTML file. For example, the first sentence could become <h1>Meet at the NASA exhibit</h1>.

When the HTML looks right but the page is still uppercase​

Paste this example into HTML source in the Phoenix HTML Viewer. Choose Preview if the source and preview appear as tabs.

<style>
  h1 { text-transform: uppercase; }
</style>
<h1>Meet at the NASA exhibit</h1>

The heading in the preview reads MEET AT THE NASA EXHIBIT. The letters between the <h1> tags still have their original spelling.

Change text-transform: uppercase; to text-transform: none;. The preview now reads Meet at the NASA exhibit. The none value lets the text display as you typed it, including the capitals in NASA. CSS text-transform

On your own site, look for text-transform in the stylesheet that applies to the heading. If the file contains several matches, check the selector before editing. The example’s h1 rule affects every first-level heading. To change only this one, give it a class such as exhibit-title and add .exhibit-title { text-transform: none; } to the stylesheet. Save, reload the page, and check another heading as well. Find text across project files in Phoenix Code

entry.title: How to Get a Hex Color From an Image and Use It in CSS
entry.summary: Pick an exact pixel from a logo, copy its hex code, and test two text colors against it. Follow along with a downloadable trail marker.
entry.content:
Suppose you want a label on your website to match the orange on a trail sign. Which orange should you copy, and will white lettering be readable on it? You can answer both questions using the picture itself. In this example the orange is #FF8C42. Dark text on it measures 7.75:1 for contrast.

Pick one pixel from the picture​

  1. Save the practice trail marker, or use your own logo. Open the Phoenix Image Color Picker, click Choose image, and select the file.
  2. Click a flat patch of orange inside the sign. Pixel magnifier shows the spot you picked. An edge pixel can be partly transparent, so move a little farther inside if you want the solid color.
  3. To pick the exact practice pixel, go to Source coordinates, enter 60 in X and 80 in Y, and click Sample pixel. The coordinates count from the top-left corner of the original image.
  4. Under Selected pixel values, find HEX / HEXA. Click the copy icon beside it. For the marker, you should get #FF8C42. If you sample X 5, Y 5 instead, you get #00000000. The final 00 means that corner is fully transparent. Return to 60, 80 before copying the orange.

Choose the lettering​

Open the Phoenix Color Contrast Checker. Paste #FF8C42 into Background and leave both color layers at full opacity. Enter each of the following values in Foreground and read the AA normal text result.

Text color on the orangeContrast ratioResult for ordinary text
White, #FFFFFF2.31:1Does not pass
Near-black, #1717177.75:1Passes

The usual WCAG AA minimum for ordinary text is 4.5:1. The white lettering can look crisp on a large graphic and still be hard to read on a small label. W3C guidance on minimum contrast

Apply the two colors to a label​

In your page’s HTML, put <span class="trail-label">Woodland loop</span> where you want the label. Add this rule to the stylesheet the page uses, then save and open the page in Live Preview.

.trail-label {
  color: #171717;
  background-color: #ff8c42;
  padding: 0.25em 0.5em;
}

You should see dark lettering on the same orange you picked from the marker. If your real label sits on a photo or uses a translucent overlay, sample and check the background behind the letters as well. Editing colors in Phoenix Code

If the logo is an SVG, you can recolor one shape in its source. If an upload form asks for a JPG, you can replace the transparent corners with your page’s background color.

entry.title: Find and fix a trailing comma in JSON
entry.summary: Use the reported line and column to find an extra comma in a JSON array or object. Try a broken example, keep the comma inside a place name, and save the corrected file.
entry.content:
In JSON, a comma tells the reader to expect another value or property. A comma immediately before the closing ] or } is a trailing comma and makes the file invalid. A comma inside quoted text is an ordinary character. Removing every comma can break the file and change your data.

Here’s how to find the extra comma in a list of stops, keep the place name Lake, north intact, and save the corrected file.

Find the error​

  1. Open the Phoenix Code JSON Formatter. Paste the example below into Input JSON. If you’re checking a file of your own, choose Open file instead.
  2. Click Validate. For this exact example, the red message points to line 3, column 39. That position is the closing square bracket. The character immediately before it is the extra comma.
{
  "walk": "Woodland loop",
  "stops": ["Oak gate", "Lake, north",],
  "open": true
}

Remove the one extra comma​

In Input JSON, replace the stops line with the one below.

  "stops": ["Oak gate", "Lake, north"],

The comma between the two stops separates two values. The comma inside "Lake, north" belongs to the name. The comma after the closing ] also stays, because the open property follows on the next line.

Click Validate again. You should see Valid JSON. Then click Format and choose Download above the result. Open formatted.json from your downloads and check that the second stop still reads "Lake, north".

What if the error points to a closing brace?​

The same rule applies to objects. For example, {"open": true,} has a comma after its last property. Change it to {"open": true}. A parser can report the closing character because that’s where it discovers the expected next value or property is missing. JSON object and array syntax.

If both versions of your file now validate and you want to see whether any values changed, compare the two JSON files.

entry.title: How to Convert Markdown to PDF with Page Breaks
entry.summary: Convert a Markdown README to a two-page PDF in your browser. Try the sample file, add a page break, and check that the table and code survive export.
entry.content:
To convert a Markdown file to PDF, open it in the Phoenix Code Markdown to PDF Converter, choose Save as PDF, then save from your browser’s print dialog. If you want a section to start on a new page, you can mark that spot in the Markdown.

Try it with a short project README. The finished handout has a file table and a CSS example on page one, followed by a checklist on page two. You can do this in a browser without installing an editor or extension.

Open the README and check the preview​

  1. Save the example Markdown file, or use a .md file of your own.
  2. Open the converter, click Open file, and select your file. If you already have the text on your clipboard, paste it into Markdown source.
  3. Under PDF page preview, look for the heading Trail Notes release handoff, a two-row table, and the CSS rule for .route-label. On a narrow screen, tap Preview to switch from the source to the rendered page.

Start the checklist on a new page​

The sample already contains a page break. For your own README, place <!-- pagebreak --> on a line by itself just before the heading you want on the next page. Leave a blank line above and below the marker. Put it outside any fenced code block so the converter reads it as an instruction.

<!-- pagebreak -->

## Before you publish

1. Open the home page.
2. Check the route label and the weekend walk link.
3. Save a copy of this handout.

In the converter preview, Before you publish still appears just below the CSS example. The print dialog shows where one sheet ends and the next begins.

Save and check the two-page PDF​

  1. In the converter toolbar, set Paper to A4 and Margins to Normal to match the example. For US Letter paper, choose Letter. If your browser shows Page numbers, turn it on to number the sheets.
  2. Click Save as PDF in the converter. In Chrome’s print dialog, choose Save as PDF under Destination. For the sample, check that the print preview shows two pages.
  3. Click Save, pick a folder, and name the file trail-notes.pdf. Open the saved PDF. On page one, search for #256347 or select the CSS rule with your mouse. Page two should begin with Before you publish.

You can check your result against the PDF saved from the example. If the checklist stayed on page one, look for a code block above the marker that still needs its closing three backticks. If your PDF includes the converter’s toolbar, use the converter’s Save as PDF button to print the document.

If you want to keep editing the README in Phoenix Code, open the original .md file there. Editing Markdown with Live Preview.

If a table cell splits at a vertical bar or the numbers are hard to compare, fix the table in the Markdown before printing. Make a Markdown table with aligned columns.

entry.title: Make a Markdown table with aligned columns
entry.summary: Build a GitHub-style Markdown table, line up distances on the right, and put a literal pipe inside a cell. Preview the example and download its HTML.
entry.content:
A Markdown table starts with a heading row and a row of dashes. A vertical bar, also called a pipe (|), separates the cells. For a numeric column, put a colon after its dashes (---:) to line up the values on the right.

Try it with a walking club’s README. The table needs to keep distances in one column and show the meeting point Gate A | East car park in a single cell.

Paste the table into a preview​

Open the Phoenix Code Markdown Viewer and paste this example into Markdown source. You can also download the example Markdown file and choose Open file. On a narrow screen, tap Preview to see the result.

# Weekend walks

| Walk | Distance (km) | Meeting point |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| Woodland loop | 4 | Gate A \| East car park |
| River path | 12 | Footbridge |

Look for three columns under Weekend walks. The 4 sits directly above the last digit of 12. The first meeting point shows a vertical bar between Gate A and East car park. The backslash is gone.

Change the alignment or add a row​

The second line of the table controls how each column looks. Use :--- for left, :---: for center, or ---: for right. Leave a blank line between a preceding paragraph and the table, and keep one stretch of dashes for each heading. GitHub’s guide to Markdown tables.

To add another walk, put this line immediately after the River path row in the source. The preview should gain a third walk, with 7 under the other distances.

| Hill climb | 7 | West gate |

If part of a cell disappears, look for a pipe in its text. In this example, changing \| to | splits the meeting point and puts East car park beyond the table’s three columns. Put the backslash back to keep the whole name together.

Save the version you need​

For a GitHub README, copy the Markdown source into README.md, save it, and use GitHub’s Preview when you edit the file there. To share a page someone can open directly in a browser, choose Download HTML in the viewer. Open the downloaded file and check the meeting point and distances once more. For a printed handout, turn your Markdown into a PDF.

If your table is already in a Word document, you can convert the file and check the cells in the same viewer. Convert a Word document to Markdown.

entry.title: How to Open an HTML File in Chrome
entry.summary: Open a local HTML file in desktop Chrome, check its images and styles, view the source, and reload a saved edit. Try it with a small practice website.
entry.content:
In desktop Chrome, press Ctrl+O on Windows or Linux, or Command+O on a Mac. Select your .html file and click Open. Chrome displays the page directly from your computer, even before you publish it.

Open a page from a folder​

  1. Find the HTML file you want to open. To follow along, download the Trail Notes practice website and extract the ZIP. Open the extracted first-website folder. Keep index.html, styles.css, and the images folder together.
  2. Click the + beside the current Chrome tab to open a new tab. Use Ctrl+O or Command+O to open the file picker. Browse to the extracted folder, select index.html, then click Open.
  3. Look for A little time outside. above an illustration of a winding trail. The address bar shows File and a path ending in first-website/index.html. Click About to open the second page, Small walks. Good stories. Use Chrome’s back arrow to return.

See the HTML and check a saved change​

To read the tags behind the page, press Ctrl+U on Windows or Linux, or Command+Option+U on a Mac. Chrome opens a second tab whose address starts with view-source:. In the sample, the line containing href="styles.css" tells Chrome which stylesheet to load. Chrome keyboard shortcuts

To change the heading, open the same index.html in a text editor such as Phoenix Code. Find <h1>A little time outside.</h1>, change the words between the tags to My weekend walks., and save the file. Return to the Home | Trail Notes tab and click Reload, the circular arrow beside the address bar. The new heading should appear.

Once the page looks right on your computer, check a phone width too. Test your website on different screen sizes

Why do I see tags or a missing image?​

  • The entire tab shows HTML tags. If the address starts with view-source:, switch back to the page tab. If the filename ends in .html.txt, Chrome is opening a text file. Save the HTML as plain text named index.html in your editor, then open that file in Chrome.
  • The heading appears, but the page looks plain or the trail is missing. Check that you extracted the whole ZIP. For this sample, styles.css belongs beside index.html, and trail.svg belongs inside images.

Can I preview just one HTML file online?​

Yes. Open the Phoenix HTML Viewer, click Open .html file, and select your file. If you see Source and Preview tabs, select Preview. The Viewer reads the chosen document. With the Trail Notes sample, it shows the heading, while the separate stylesheet and illustration stay in your project folder. To see the complete sample, open the local index.html directly in Chrome. Troubleshoot missing CSS, images, or JavaScript in the Viewer

entry.title: How to Test Your Website on Different Screen Sizes
entry.summary: Preview one HTML page at desktop, tablet, and phone widths. Find the card that makes the phone scroll sideways, fix its CSS, and check all three sizes again.
entry.content:
The Woodland loop card below fits on a laptop and a tablet. On a phone, the distance disappears off the right edge. Try the three screen widths in the free Phoenix HTML Viewer, then add one line of CSS to bring 2 miles back into view.

Open the same page at three widths​

  1. Open the Phoenix HTML Viewer. Paste the whole example below into HTML source, replacing any text already there. If you see separate Source and Preview tabs, paste into Source and switch to Preview.
  2. Under Rendered preview, open the screen-width menu. It initially reads Responsive. Select Desktop, then Tablet, then Mobile. Look for 2 miles on the right of the green card each time.
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Weekend walks</title>
  <style>
    body { margin: 0; font: 18px/1.5 system-ui, sans-serif; }
    .walk {
      box-sizing: border-box;
      width: 720px;
      padding: 24px;
      color: #173c32;
      background: #e5f2e8;
    }
    .distance { float: right; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <main class="walk">
    <strong class="distance">2 miles</strong>
    <h1>Woodland loop</h1>
    <p>Start at the old oak and follow the green signs.</p>
  </main>
</body>
</html>
Viewport presetWhat you should see
Desktop, 1280 pixelsThe full green card and some white space to its right.
Tablet, 768 pixelsThe full card, with a much smaller gap on the right.
Mobile, 390 pixelsThe heading is visible. You have to scroll sideways inside the preview to reach 2 miles.

Fix the card and test again​

In HTML source, find width: 720px; inside the .walk rule. Keep that line and add the following one immediately below it.

max-width: 100%;

Switch back to Preview if needed. At Mobile, the distance and heading should now be visible together. The description wraps to a second line. Switch back to Tablet and Desktop. The card still stops at 720 pixels on those wider screens.

The card needed 720 pixels even when its parent had only 390. The new maximum lets it shrink to the available width. The existing box-sizing: border-box keeps the padding inside that width. On your own page, apply the change to the element that sticks out, save the stylesheet, and repeat the same width checks. How CSS max-width works

For a page with a sidebar, you can also move the two columns into reading order on a phone. Build a responsive CSS Grid sidebar.

Test a project with separate files​

If your HTML links to a local stylesheet or images, open the whole project in Phoenix Code so Live Preview can find those files. In Phoenix Pro, the device-size button at the right of the Live Preview toolbar lets you switch widths. After checking the layout, open your published page on a real phone to try the links, touch controls, and on-screen keyboard. Device Preview in Phoenix Pro · Troubleshoot missing styles and images

entry.title: Why a Unix timestamp shows 1970 in JavaScript
entry.summary: Compare Unix timestamps in seconds and milliseconds, fix a JavaScript date that lands in 1970, and read the same event in UTC and local time.
entry.content:
Suppose a log says an event happened at 1735689600. You expect January 1, 2025, but new Date(1735689600) gives you a date in January 1970. That log counts seconds since January 1, 1970 at midnight UTC. JavaScript expects milliseconds when you pass a number to new Date().

There are 1,000 milliseconds in a second. You can check the units in a browser before changing any code.

Check the same instant two ways​

Open the Phoenix Code Unix Timestamp Converter. Under Timestamp to Date, enter each number in turn, click Convert, and look at ISO 8601 in the result. The final Z means the time is in UTC.

Number you enterUnits in this exampleISO 8601 result
1735689600Seconds2025-01-01T00:00:00.000Z
1735689600000Milliseconds2025-01-01T00:00:00.000Z
1735689600123Milliseconds, 123 ms after midnight2025-01-01T00:00:00.123Z

The first two numbers identify the same instant. For a value from your own system, check the field description for seconds or milliseconds. A number’s length is a clue for recent dates. The documented units also work for older dates and values close to zero.

Pass milliseconds to JavaScript​

If the field contains seconds, multiply by 1,000 once. If the field already contains milliseconds, pass the number through directly. Try these lines in a browser console or your JavaScript file. JavaScript Date constructor.

const logSeconds = 1735689600;
const logMilliseconds = 1735689600123;

console.log(new Date(logSeconds).toISOString());        // 1970-01-21T02:08:09.600Z
console.log(new Date(logSeconds * 1000).toISOString()); // 2025-01-01T00:00:00.000Z
console.log(new Date(logMilliseconds).toISOString());   // 2025-01-01T00:00:00.123Z

Why local time can show the previous day​

For the first example, UTC shows midnight on January 1. With the browser set to New York, Local Time shows 7 p.m. on December 31. New York was five hours behind UTC at that instant. Your local result depends on your time zone. When comparing events from two machines, compare their ISO values including the Z and any fractional seconds.

entry.title: How to Convert WebP to JPG and Choose the Background Color
entry.summary: Convert a transparent WebP to a JPG with a white or custom background. Compare two actual downloads and see when to keep a transparent PNG instead.
entry.content:
A logo can float over any page color as a transparent WebP. A JPG needs a color in every pixel. If an upload form requires JPG, choose the background before adding the file. These two images came from the same WebP. Only the background setting changed.

White backgroundDark green background

Download a JPG with the background you want​

  1. Open the Phoenix WebP to JPG Converter. Use your own WebP, or download the transparent trail marker to follow along.
  2. Leave Image quality at 90% for this example. Under Background color, keep white (#FFFFFF) for the first result, or click the color swatch and choose the color you want behind the image. We used dark green (#21392F) for the second version.
  3. Click Choose files and select the WebP. Conversion starts when you select it. In Your JPG files, use the download button on the row for your image.
  4. Open the downloaded trail-marker.jpg. The marker still measures 240 × 160 pixels. Look at the four corners to see the chosen background. If you want another version, set the new color and add the original WebP again.

Why does the white box stay?​

Check which file you added. If you start the second conversion with the white JPG, the white corners are already part of the picture. Go back to the original transparent WebP. The background setting fills transparent pixels. It leaves an opaque white area in a photo or logo in place.

The quality slider controls JPG compression. Increasing it won’t restore transparency, and decreasing it can soften the sharp edges of lettering. Compare the downloaded file at the size visitors will see it. Image formats and transparency

Keep the transparent corners​

If the same logo must sit on both light and dark pages, keep the original WebP or open it in the Phoenix WebP to PNG Converter. Choose the original file and download the PNG. In our practice export, the corner pixel stayed fully transparent. You can check your own file by sampling a corner in the image color picker walkthrough.

entry.title: Why Your HTML Preview Is Missing CSS, Images or JavaScript
entry.summary: Fix CSS not loading, missing images and JavaScript that won't run in an HTML preview. Check file paths and permissions with working examples.
entry.content:
An HTML file can link to CSS, images, and JavaScript without copying those files into it. If a preview is missing styles or images, first check the file paths and the preview permissions. If a button does nothing, check whether scripts are allowed. This guide also helps when CSS is not loading, HTML images are not showing, or JavaScript is not working in HTML.

The examples below use Phoenix HTML Viewer. HTML and CSS written inside the document work by default. Hosted files and JavaScript each need permission in the Viewer. The Viewer reads the HTML file you open; it does not import the files beside it.

You will need: your HTML text or an .html file. The Viewer is free and runs in your browser. For the last steps, keep any separate CSS, JavaScript, and image files with your HTML. You can use file editing and Live Preview. These features are in both Phoenix Pro and the free Community edition.

Identify what is missing​

What you seeFirst checkNext step
Hosted CSS is not loadingIs external access enabled?For trusted content, turn on Allow external resources. Then try the hosted example.
A local styles.css file is not loadingDid you open only the HTML file?Open the full project folder in Phoenix Code.
An image is not showingIs its address a hosted URL or a local path?Check the path and filename.
A hosted file still does not loadWhat URL did the browser request?Check the failed request.
A button does nothingIs JavaScript allowed?Test a small inline script before you debug a bigger one.

If the stylesheet loads but the page still looks wrong, check whether the CSS rule targets the right element or another rule overrides it. For a heading that stays in capitals, compare the HTML text with its CSS text-transform rule.

Test HTML and inline CSS​

  1. Open the HTML Viewer.
  2. Click inside HTML source and paste the complete document below, replacing any sample text already there. It needs no downloaded stylesheet, image, or JavaScript.
<!doctype html>
<html lang='en'>
<head>
  <meta charset='utf-8'>
  <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1'>
  <title>Preview check</title>
  <style>
    body {
      background: #f4f6f8;
      padding: 24px;
    }
    p {
      color: #164ea6;
      font-size: 20px;
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <p>HTML and inline CSS are working.</p>
</body>
</html>
  1. Look at the Rendered preview panel. On a narrow screen, switch from Source to Preview to see the result.

You should see a blue paragraph on a pale background.

If this works, add parts of your original page a little at a time: HTML first, then styles, images, and scripts. When the preview breaks, check the last part you added.

To check your own file, choose Open .html file above the source editor. This replaces the current source. To keep your edits, use Download .html in the source toolbar first. On desktop, this is the download-arrow button with that tooltip.

To see a saved page with the CSS and images beside it on your computer, open the local HTML file in Chrome.

If changes stop appearing, check whether Live preview is on. Its checkbox and Allow external resources are above the editor on a wide screen. On a narrow screen, open Preview settings below the workspace. When Live preview is off, use Refresh preview after you edit.

Keep local files in the expected folders​

For a working example, download the image-and-text practice project used in our image layout tutorial. Extract the ZIP first. Keep these files together in the extracted folder:

image-text-layout/
├── index.html
├── styles.css
└── images/
    └── woodland.jpg

Inside index.html, a stylesheet reference belongs in the head:

<link rel='stylesheet' href='styles.css'>

An image reference belongs where the image should appear in the body:

<img src='images/woodland.jpg' alt='A sunlit path between tall trees'
  width='1200' height='675'>

The first path expects styles.css beside the HTML file. The second expects woodland.jpg inside an images folder. Check that the filenames and case match the files you have. For your own project, use your image's filename, dimensions, and description.

Opening only index.html in the Viewer leaves those files behind. Allow external resources cannot give the Viewer access to other files on your computer. Keep the files together and use the full-project workflow below.

If the missing image is the small icon in the browser tab, follow Add a favicon in HTML to check it on both the home page and a nested page.

Check hosted URLs and relative paths​

A full URL such as https://example.com/images/logo.png points to a file on a website. This is an example URL; replace it with your own image URL when testing. Hosted images, stylesheets, and fonts need Allow external resources in the Viewer.

An image address that starts with data:image/ carries the image inside the HTML. If that image is missing, test the complete data URL with a working Base64 image.

To see the difference, replace the Viewer source with this complete example. It loads the same practice stylesheet and woodland photo from the docs website:

<!doctype html>
<html lang='en'>
<head>
  <meta charset='utf-8'>
  <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1'>
  <title>Hosted resource check</title>
  <link rel='stylesheet'
    href='https://docs.phcode.dev/tutorials/image-text-layout/styles.css'>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>A woodland walk</h1>
  <div class='feature'>
    <img
      src='https://docs.phcode.dev/tutorials/image-text-layout/images/woodland.jpg'
      alt='A sunlit path between tall trees' width='320' height='180'>
  </div>
</body>
</html>
  1. With Allow external resources off, the heading is unstyled and the photo does not load.
  2. Turn on Allow external resources for this example. You should see a dark green heading, a pale background, and the woodland photo. Leave scripts off; this example needs only HTML, CSS, and an image.

The photo is by Johannes Plenio on Unsplash, as credited in the practice project. This example uses complete hosted addresses; it does not access files on your computer.

A relative path starts from another location. For paths in your HTML:

  • styles.css and ./styles.css resolve from the current directory.
  • ../styles.css resolves from the parent directory.
  • On an HTTP or HTTPS page, the browser resolves /styles.css from the site root, even when the page is in a subfolder.

A relative path does not mean 'find this file anywhere on my computer.' MDN explains how relative references are resolved.

For a background image in an external CSS file, a relative url(...) starts from the stylesheet's location, which may be a different folder from the HTML file.

If a hosted file still will not load​

Permission alone will not fix a wrong URL or a missing file. Open the image or stylesheet URL in a new tab. It should show the image or CSS itself, not a sign-in screen or a sharing page.

To see what the preview actually requested in Chrome on desktop:

  1. Open Chrome's three-dot menu, then More tools > Developer tools. Select Network in the developer tools panel.
  2. In the Viewer, turn Live preview off and click Refresh preview. Keep Allow external resources on only for content you trust.
  3. Find the image or CSS request in Network. Select it and open Headers to check Request URL and Status Code.
What you findWhat to check
404The server could not find that URL. Check the filename, case, and folder path.
A blocked requestRead the browser's Console message for the reason. Renaming the file will not fix a preview restriction.
200, but the page is still unstyledCheck that the response contains the expected CSS, then check which rules apply to the element.

Chrome's Network guide explains the request details. Turn Live preview back on when you are done. External resources can contact other websites, so leave them off for HTML you do not trust. Do not disable browser security to make a preview work.

Test a button with inline JavaScript​

Paste the first, self-contained example back into the Viewer. Add this button after the paragraph, just before the closing </body> tag. Start with Allow external resources off.

<button type='button' onclick='this.textContent=`Clicked`'>
  Test button
</button>

With scripts off, the button appears, but clicking it does not change its label. Turn on Allow external resources, then select Run scripts — enable external resources first. Click the Test button in the preview again; its label should change to Clicked.

Changing these permission settings refreshes the preview and resets the button. Click it again after you change a setting.

This tests JavaScript written inside the HTML. In pasted HTML, the Viewer can run inline scripts, but it blocks external <script src> files and fetch/XHR requests.

To test a small example with a separate stylesheet or script, open the online HTML editor. Paste your HTML, CSS and JavaScript into the index.html, style.css and script.js tabs.

For a project with more files or modules, open the full folder in an editor. If it also needs a backend server, run that server too.

If your own inline script still fails, open the developer tools Console. Fix the first error from your script, then test again.

Open the complete project in Phoenix Code​

For a complete editing workspace, use Phoenix Code. Work on your HTML, CSS and JavaScript files together, with Live Preview alongside your code.

For HTML that links to local CSS, images, or scripts, use Phoenix Code's project workflow. Follow the extracted practice project above. Open its original index.html, which uses local paths. The hosted example above was only for testing resource permissions.

For your own project:

  1. If you edited the document in the Viewer, use Download .html to save it. This downloads the HTML source; it does not collect referenced images or stylesheets.
  2. Keep that HTML file with its CSS, JavaScript, and images in the folders its paths point to.
  3. Open Phoenix Code on desktop, or use its browser app in Chrome or Edge for local-folder access.
  4. In the Start Project Dialog, choose Open Folder and select the folder containing the HTML file. If the dialog is closed, click the folder icon at the top left to open it again. The project files should appear in the file list.
  5. Click your HTML file in the file list. If the preview is hidden, click the lightning bolt at the top of the right toolbar to show Live Preview.
  6. If Phoenix Code asks whether you trust the project, choose Trust & Execute Preview only for a project you trust.
  7. Fix any incorrect paths in the HTML and use File > Save File. In Live Preview, check that the stylesheet changes the page and the image loads.

The Viewer link does not transfer your project. Save your edited HTML in its project folder, then open that folder in Phoenix Code.

In the practice project, opening index.html should show Plan a woodland walk, the forest photo, and Take the scenic route. To arrange that photo beside its text, continue with the image-and-text layout tutorial.

Q&A​

Question: Why does inline CSS work in the HTML Viewer, but my separate styles.css file does not?

Short answer: Inline CSS is part of the HTML document you paste or open, so the Viewer can render it right away. A separate local styles.css file is not loaded when you open only the HTML file. If your page uses local CSS, images, or JavaScript files, keep them in the right folders. Open the full project folder in Phoenix Code instead of just opening the HTML file in the Viewer.

Question: Does Allow external resources make local files on my computer available to the preview?

Short answer: No. Allow external resources lets the Viewer load hosted resources from websites, such as full image or stylesheet URLs. It does not give the Viewer access to other files beside your HTML on your computer. For local files like styles.css or images/woodland.jpg, use the full-project workflow and open the folder that contains all related files.

Question: What should I check first when an image does not appear?

Short answer: First check whether the image uses a hosted URL or a local relative path. For hosted images, make sure Allow external resources is enabled and that the URL opens the actual image, not a sign-in page or a sharing page. For local images, make sure the filename, case, and folder path match exactly. Remember, a relative path does not search your entire computer.

Question: Why does my button show up but not respond when clicked?

Short answer: The button may rely on JavaScript, and scripts are off by default in the Viewer. For trusted content, enable Allow external resources first, then enable Run scripts — enable external resources first. If inline JavaScript still fails, open the browser developer tools Console, fix the first script error shown there, and test again.

Question: When should I switch from the HTML Viewer to Phoenix Code?

Short answer: Use the HTML Viewer for quick checks with pasted HTML, inline CSS, hosted resources, or small inline JavaScript tests. Use Phoenix Code when your page needs local CSS, images, JavaScript files, modules, or a full folder structure. Phoenix Code's project workflow lets Live Preview resolve local paths from the project folder.

entry.title: How to Convert PNG to PDF for Free Online
entry.summary: Combine PNG images into one PDF in your browser. Arrange pages, choose paper settings and download without uploading your images or creating an account.
entry.content:
You can turn a PNG screenshot, scanned page or diagram into a PDF without installing software. The Phoenix Code PNG to PDF converter combines still PNG images into one file, with one image per page. Conversion runs locally in your browser, and the downloaded PDF has no watermark. No account or subscription is required.

This guide walks through choosing images, arranging pages and saving the result. For color, resolution and printing details, see what PNG-to-PDF conversion preserves.

Watch a complete conversion​

Follow along with Try an example in the converter. This walkthrough drags the parrot above the coastal picture, chooses A4 with 10 mm margins, and opens the downloaded PDF in Chrome's PDF viewer. Select Choose PNG files when you are ready to use your own images.

Open video

1. Choose your PNG images​

Open the PNG to PDF converter, select Choose PNG files, and pick one or more still PNG images from your device. On a computer, you can also drop PNG files into the converter or paste PNG images from the clipboard.

On a phone, use the file picker to choose your images. If your phone saved a photo in another format, first obtain a PNG version: this converter does not accept every image format, and renaming a file's extension does not convert it.

The tool checks each image before it can be included. If a file has an error, read its message and remove or replace it. Every remaining image must be ready before Create PDF becomes available.

Damaged or unsupported color information, including unsupported HDR data, produces a specific error. Export a copy as a standard sRGB PNG and try again, keeping your original file.

2. Put the pages in order​

Each image becomes one PDF page. The order of the cards is the order of the pages in the finished file.

  • With a mouse, drag from the image preview, filename or empty space on a card.
  • On a touch screen, press and hold a card briefly, then drag it. A normal swipe still scrolls the page.
  • Use Move up and Move down when you prefer buttons.
  • With a keyboard, focus a card and press Enter or Space. Choose its position with the arrow keys, Home or End, then press Enter or Space again. Escape cancels the move.

The card's action buttons retain their own actions. You can remove an unwanted image without restarting the whole batch.

3. Choose paper and background settings​

The settings affect every page, with automatic orientation determined separately for each image when a paper size is selected.

SettingWhat to choose
Page sizeFit to image for a page based on each image's dimensions and stored print resolution; A4 or US Letter for standard paper.
OrientationWith A4 or US Letter, choose Automatic, Portrait or Landscape. Fit to image determines the page shape from the image.
MarginsChoose none, 5 mm, 10 mm or 20 mm. Images fit inside the available area without cropping or stretching.
Transparent areasChoose White to give transparent image areas a white background, or Transparent to retain transparency.

Fit to image uses the PNG's stored print resolution and adds the selected margins. If no resolution is stored, it uses 96 pixels per inch. For example, a 2400-pixel-wide PNG stored at 300 pixels per inch occupies 8 inches before margins. A4 and US Letter fit the image to the chosen paper, changing its printed size while keeping the original pixel dimensions.

Stored image orientation and pixel aspect ratios are respected. If the stored resolution would make an image-sized PDF page too large or too small, choose A4 or US Letter and create the PDF again.

4. Check the layout, create the PDF and save it​

The page previews show orientation, margins and image placement. They use smaller preview images, so use them to check the layout rather than fine detail or final color.

Select Create PDF and keep the browser tab open while it works. When the PDF is ready, select Download PDF to save it to your device. Open that downloaded file to check page order, readability and appearance before printing or sharing it.

Each picture is a separate page; your PDF viewer may show the pages one below another. If you keep Fit to image, the pages follow your images' dimensions instead of the A4 paper shown in the video.

Changing the page order or settings after creation requires creating the PDF again. Your original PNG files stay on your device.

How many images can you combine?​

All of these limits apply together:

LimitMaximum
Images100 still PNG files
Individual file50 MB
Total input files200 MB
Pixels in one image24 megapixels
Pixels across the batch48 megapixels
Either image dimension16,384 pixels
Finished PDF128 MB

A batch of large scans may reach the pixel or output limit before it reaches 100 images. Available device memory can also limit a conversion. If a batch fails, try fewer or smaller images and keep the tab open.

What happens to your files?​

The tool uses browser memory to process the images and generate the PDF. It does not upload your images or PDF to a conversion server or save them in persistent browser storage. The page still loads website code and other assets.

Your original PNG files and downloaded PDF remain on your device. Closing the tab does not delete them. If you are sharing a sensitive document, check the contents of the downloaded PDF and the destination before sending it.

Can the PDF text be searched or copied?​

This tool creates image-based PDF pages. Text in a screenshot remains part of the image; the converter does not perform optical character recognition (OCR). Use an OCR tool if you need a searchable or selectable text layer.

When your images are ready, open the PNG to PDF converter and create your file. If you plan to print it, first read how pixel dimensions, color and paper size affect the result.

entry.title: PNG to PDF Quality: Pixels, Color and Print Size
entry.summary: Understand PNG-to-PDF image quality: original pixels, bit depth, color profiles, transparency, stored print resolution and paper-size settings.
entry.content:
Converting a PNG to PDF can preserve image detail, but “no quality loss” needs a precise meaning. Pixel dimensions, color profiles, bit depth and print size are different properties. Preserving one does not guarantee that all the others stay unchanged.

The Phoenix Code PNG to PDF converter preserves original PNG pixel values, dimensions and bit depth, including 16-bit images. It uses lossless compression and copies supported embedded color profiles into the PDF. Fit to image also uses stored print resolution. PDF readers, screens and printers can still affect how colors look, so check the downloaded file and keep your source PNGs.

What the converter preserves​

PropertyBehavior in this converter
Image pixels and dimensionsOriginal pixel values and dimensions are kept. A 2400 × 1600 image remains 2400 × 1600 pixels in the PDF.
CompressionLossless image compression is used. Compression does not automatically mean loss of detail.
Color and bit depthOriginal bit depth, including 16-bit values, is kept. Supported embedded color profiles are copied into the PDF. Colors without color information are treated as sRGB.
TransparencyCan be retained with Transparent, or placed on white with White.
Stored print resolutionUsed by Fit to image, with a 96-pixels-per-inch fallback when no resolution is stored. Standard paper sizes change the print scale.
Stored orientationApplied to the image's placement. Rotated or mirrored images keep their intended orientation.
Other image metadataNot copied into the PDF.
Image placementThe image fits within the chosen paper and margins without cropping or stretching.
Text in screenshotsRemains an image. No searchable or editable OCR text layer is created.

Lossless compression stores the original image samples without discarding detail. The PDF has its own structure, so its file size can be larger than the source PNG. The small browser previews remain layout aids; use the downloaded PDF to inspect fine detail and color.

Supported RGB and grayscale ICC profiles are copied unchanged. Standard sRGB and SDR Display P3 color information are also supported. Images with no color information use an sRGB assumption. Damaged or unsupported color information, including unsupported HDR data, produces an error. If this happens, export a standard sRGB PNG copy and try again, keeping the original for any work that needs its unsupported color data.

Pixel dimensions and print size are different​

The number of pixels alone does not determine how large an image prints. Its physical size also matters. Effective pixels per inch (PPI) are calculated as:

PPI = pixels along one side ÷ printed inches along that side.

For example, an image that is 2400 pixels wide provides:

Printed widthEffective resolution
8 inches300 PPI
12 inches200 PPI
25 inches96 PPI

These are arithmetic examples, not a guarantee that a particular image meets a printer's requirements. Check the required physical dimensions and resolution for the intended print job.

Changing paper size does not create more detail. A larger placement spreads the same pixels over a larger area; a smaller placement brings them closer together.

Choose a page size for the intended use​

The walkthrough starts with the converter's landscape sample already added. It shows the paper, margin and transparency choices, then shows the downloaded PDF in Chrome's PDF viewer. To follow along, choose Try an example in the converter and remove the coastal picture, leaving the parrot.

Open video

Fit to image​

Use Fit to image when you want each PDF page sized from that image's pixel dimensions and stored print resolution. The tool uses the PNG's resolution information, falling back to valid EXIF resolution and then to 96 pixels per inch when no resolution is available. Selected margins add space around the image.

A 2400-pixel-wide image stored at 300 pixels per inch occupies 8 inches before margins. The same image without stored resolution uses 96 pixels per inch and occupies 25 inches. Horizontal and vertical resolution can differ; the converter respects both, along with stored pixel aspect ratios and orientation.

The resolution setting is often called DPI in image software. Keeping that setting preserves the intended print scale, while actual print quality still depends on the source image, PDF reader and printer. If the stored resolution would create a page that is too large or too small, choose A4 or US Letter and create the PDF again.

A4 or US Letter​

Choose A4 or US Letter when the receiving person or printer expects standard paper. Automatic orientation chooses portrait or landscape separately for each image; you can also select either orientation yourself.

The image fits inside the selected margins without cropping or stretching. This changes its printed size and effective PPI to fit the paper. If its proportions differ from the page, unused space remains. Selecting no margins does not guarantee edge-to-edge coverage on a differently shaped page, and a physical printer may impose its own unprintable borders.

Understand transparent backgrounds​

Choose Transparent to retain transparent image areas, or White to place them on white. The checkerboard in the converter is only a preview aid; it is not added to the PDF.

PDF readers usually display transparent pages on white. A white-looking page in a reader therefore does not, by itself, tell you whether image transparency was flattened. Check the downloaded PDF in the application where you intend to use it.

Check the downloaded PDF, not just the preview​

The converter's small previews show page layout. They are not a full-resolution proof of fine detail or color.

After selecting Create PDF and Download PDF, open the saved file and check:

  1. Page order and placement. Confirm that every intended image appears and that the paper, orientation and margins are suitable.
  2. Fine detail. Inspect important text or lines at a useful viewing scale. Raster images can show pixels when magnified far enough, even when their pixel dimensions are preserved.
  3. Color and transparency. Compare the result in the application you will actually use. Supported profiles and bit depth are preserved, but viewer and printer color management can affect appearance. Keep the original PNG for future editing or metadata you may need.
  4. Print size. Check the PDF page dimensions and the printer's scaling settings. A viewer's “fit to page” print option can change the physical size again.

Common questions about quality​

Why is my PDF larger than the original PNGs?​

A PDF has its own document structure and image representation. Transparency and image content also affect the output size. This tool does not guarantee a smaller file. The output limit is 128 MB; try a smaller batch if you reach it.

Does local processing guarantee identical colors?​

No. Processing location and color handling are separate questions. This converter preserves original pixel values, bit depth and supported color profiles while processing locally. The PDF reader, screen profile, printer, paper and print settings can still affect the visible result. Untagged images use an sRGB assumption; check the downloaded PDF in your intended viewing or printing workflow.

Can I make a low-resolution screenshot sharper by converting it?​

Conversion does not recover missing detail. Start with a higher-resolution original when possible. Enlarging a small raster image spreads the existing pixels over a larger area.

Does changing margins resize the embedded image?​

With Fit to image, margins add space around the image without changing its printed size. With A4 or US Letter, margins change the area available for the image and therefore its printed size. The embedded pixel dimensions stay the same in either case.

For the complete selection, ordering and download workflow, follow the free PNG to PDF conversion guide. You can then open the converter and choose settings for your actual sharing or printing task.

entry.title: Phoenix Code 5.5.11: Layers, Visual AI & ChatGPT Codex
entry.summary: See and edit your page’s HTML structure, try design ideas with Phoenix AI, and bring ChatGPT Codex and Claude Code CLI into a visual workflow. Plus simpler AI setup, demos, usage graphs, and photo search.
entry.content:
Phoenix Code 5.5.11 is now available at phcode.dev.

See and edit your HTML with the new Layers panel, try AI design ideas on your page, explore interactive replies in chat, and bring your existing CLI agents into Phoenix Code. There’s also simpler AI setup, AI demos, usage graphs, thinking effort, and photo search.

Explore and Edit Your Page with Layers​

Edit your web pages visually, without touching code! The new Layers sidebar lets you explore your page’s HTML structure, add, move, duplicate, or delete elements, and edit their properties.

Change colors, fonts, sizes, and spacing with simple visual controls. Every change is instantly reflected in your code and Live Preview.

The Layers panel is a Phoenix Pro feature.

Ask AI in Live Preview​

Just point and ask AI, instead of explaining what you want to change! Select any part of your page in Live Preview and ask AI to make changes. No need to describe where or what you're referring to.

Ask AI to suggest alternative designs, explore color schemes, or try different fonts.

Ask AI also works with custom server previews, including PHP and other server-rendered pages, as well as selected code or Markdown text.

Available only in desktop apps.

Intelligent UI in AI Chat​

See what AI means, instead of just reading about it! Phoenix AI can now show interactive designs, buttons, cards, layouts, and more directly in chat.

Explore different styles, click through options, and adjust controls right in the conversation. Instead of just describing an idea, AI can show you how it looks and works—all without opening Live Preview or writing code.

This feature is available only in desktop apps.

Bring Your Claude Code & Codex CLI to Phoenix Code​

Supercharge your existing CLI agents with rich, interactive visual workflows! Use your existing Claude Code or Codex subscriptions in Phoenix Code to explore designs in Live Preview, try interactive options, and make changes visually instead of relying on text descriptions.

Run multiple CLI sessions, switch between them easily, and send Ask AI requests directly to your agents. Track your AI consumption with the built-in AI Usage Meter (see below).

Running CLI agents inside Phoenix Code is a Phoenix Pro feature, available only in desktop apps.

Track Your AI Usage​

See how much AI you're using, all in one place! Track token usage and estimated costs across Phoenix AI, Claude Code, and Codex CLI sessions.

Explore daily usage graphs, monthly trends, and breakdowns by AI model. You can also clear your usage history without deleting your chats.

Costs are estimated using API list prices and may differ from your actual provider charges. Available only in desktop apps.

Easier AI Setup & Quick Access​

Get started with your favorite AI tools more easily! The new AI start screen brings Phoenix AI, ChatGPT Codex, and Claude Code CLI together in one place.

Quickly set up your AI tools, switch running sessions, and pick up right where you left off.

AI Demos​

See what you can create with Phoenix AI before signing in or using any AI credits. Watch a page take shape, explore the result, and reveal the prompt behind it. Click Surprise Me to try it.

This feature is available only in desktop apps.

Adjust AI Thinking Effort​

Choose how much effort AI puts into solving your problems! Use lower thinking effort for quick, simple tasks or higher effort for complex problems that need deeper reasoning.

Select your preferred Thinking Effort for supported AI models, or leave it at Default to use the model's standard setting.

This feature is available only in desktop apps.

Discover Stock Photos with AI​

Find the perfect photos for your website with the help of AI! Explore real stock photos, discover new ideas, and let AI help you narrow down your choices to find images that fit your design.

Ask AI to add your favorite photos directly to your page or download them into your project.

This feature is available only in desktop apps.

Larger Image Previews in Markdown​

Take a closer look at images without leaving your Markdown document! Open images in a larger view to see details more clearly, whether you're reading or editing.

Simply click an image in reader mode, or double-click it while editing. Press Escape to return to your document.

Terminal and Git improvements​

  • Name your terminals. Rename terminal tabs so you can tell your development server, build, and shell apart.
  • Keep your bearings after a project switch. A notice lets you keep existing terminals running or restart them in the new project's folder, with confirmation when active processes would be stopped.
  • Open terminal links. Applications that print clickable terminal hyperlinks can now open them in your default browser.
  • See what has been pushed. Git history marks the last pushed commit and identifies the local commits above it. Branches that have not been pushed get a clear indication too.
  • Open projects without Git interruptions. Projects without a repository no longer trigger a “getting remotes” error dialog.

Notable fixes and performance improvements​

  • Fixed a race where a delayed file reload could overwrite text typed or saved while the reload was in progress. (Change)
  • Fixed stale Markdown preview updates reverting newer edits made in the code editor. (Change)
  • Live Preview reconnects after a dropped connection, and incomplete HTML is handled more reliably while you type. (Reconnect, HTML editing)
  • Reduced repeated CSS parsing, page measurements, and tree rebuilding during selection and editing in Live Preview and Layers.
  • Fixed JavaScript hints getting stuck while indexing HTML or PHP, and older project preferences arriving after a project switch. (Hints, Preferences)
  • Python and PHP language-server setup now limits automatic retries and keeps error details and a manual retry available in the task list. Python tooling also updates to Pyrefly 1.2.0 and Ruff 0.16.5. (Setup, Tooling)
  • Fixed the sidebar resize handle being left over the editor after the sidebar was collapsed. (Change)
  • Dropping several files now leaves the last file in the drop order active, regardless of which one loads fastest. (Change)
  • Notifications stay open while you hover over them, giving you time to read or use their actions. (Change)
  • AI plan review now handles approval, revision, cancellation, and stopping more consistently. Chat also resumes following new messages after you have scrolled back to read older replies.

Platform and account notes​

  • Windows: Fixed AI multiline edits being rejected when the file and the AI used different line endings. Language-server quick fixes also handle drive-letter capitalization correctly.
  • macOS: Improved semibold and bold text rendering in the interface.
  • Managed desktop installations: Administrators can point the updater at a custom update manifest, including a custom Linux installer URL.
  • Accounts: Desktop sign-in refreshes Pro access immediately, and existing subscribers no longer receive prompts to buy Pro again.

Get the update at phcode.dev, and let us know what you build in GitHub Discussions.
